candidates.title: Norfolk Southern awards $100,000 to Atlanta food bank
candidates.excerpt: ATLANTA — Norfolk Southern has awarded a $100,000 grant to the Atlanta Community Food Bank, the railroad has announced. The award, part of NS’ Thriving Communities Grant Program, will support the Food Bank’s School Pantry Program, which expands access to food for children and families, and to child nutrition initiatives. NS support for the Food Bank includes more than 200 hours of volunteer work by employees to sort food and prepare distribution to those in need during fiscal 2025. The Thriving Communities program supports nonprofit organizations across the 22-state NS network. — To report news or errors, contact trainsnewswire@firecrown.com.

candidates.title: Freightos Weekly Update: Red Sea container traffic set for full return in Q1
candidates.excerpt: Trends in international ocean logistics seem even more confusing than usual lately: more Iranian attacks but more Hormuz traffic; more crude exports but oil prices still around $100 per barrel; more risk of Houthi attacks on passing ships, but more container vessels returning to the Red Sea anyway. Iran has stepped up the frequency of attacks on vessels around the Strait of Hormuz, partially because transits and crude flows through the waterway have increased in recent weeks. Last week an Iranian projectile sunk a Dubai-linked container vessel, indicating that even some container ships are taking the risk of transiting the strait, though most traffic still comprises tankers. Despite some estimates that the increase in tankers exiting the Persian Gulf is contributing to Middle East crude exports approaching pre-war levels, crude prices – still pricing in elevated risk – remain high. candidates.title: The empty container problem isn’t a shortage. It’s a data problem.
candidates.excerpt: Container shipping has just lived through its third consecutive year of a peak season that arrived early and left just as fast. Shippers rushed cargo out ahead of the July 1 bunker adjustment factor reset, itself a product of fuel costs pushed up by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, continued avoidance of the Red Sea cut effective fleet capacity by around 12%, with slow steaming absorbing another 2%, according to MPC Container Ships chief executive Constantin Baack. Idle capacity opened 2026 at just 0.6% of the global fleet. When ships run this close to full utilization, there’s no cushion left for the equipment side, either. A terminal that’s short on boxes during a front-loading rush can be sitting on a surplus a few weeks later, paying storage and demurrage on equipment nobody is ready to move. candidates.title: Project Cargo East of Suez: Routing Oversized Freight When the Short Way Is Not Simple
candidates.excerpt: Since late 2023, attacks on merchant shipping around the southern Red Sea have changed how many carriers route between Asia, the Red Sea, the Gulf and East Africa. Much of the public discussion has focused on standard containers and headline freight rates. For shippers of project and oversized cargo, such as machinery, generators, steel structures and plant modules, the change has been more awkward. Their cargo depends on special equipment, careful planning and fewer options. This piece does not try to predict when conditions will change. It sets out the practical questions we now work through on every out-of-gauge file headed to these regions. Suez or the Cape: a decision made shipment by shipment For cargo moving between Asia and Europe or the Mediterranean, many carriers have chosen the Cape of Good Hope over the Suez Canal. Global terminal operators, backed by container shipping groups, are keenly eyeing fresh concessions at Sri Lanka’s Colombo port, according to industry sources. One opportunity up for grabs soon is a rebid for South Asia Gateway Terminals (SAGT), where 30-year concession rights end in 2029. SAGT’s ownership has four partners: 42% held by John Keells Holdings; 33% by Maersk/APMT; 15% by Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA); and 10% by Evergreen. According to sources in Colombo, Sri Lankan policymakers are not considering a further extension of the concession term but will seek new proposals. “There are clear signals that SLPA will go in for a fresh tendering attempt,” one source told The Loadstar. candidates.title: Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years
candidates.excerpt: Iraq’s national shipping line is returning to scheduled container services in the Gulf after more than half a century, as the country seeks to rebuild maritime connections disrupted by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. According to Alphaliner, Iraqi Maritime Line is deploying the 902 teu Basrah on an eight-day shuttle linking Jebel Ali in Dubai with Umm Qasr, Iraq’s principal container gateway. The first sailing was scheduled to depart Jebel Ali yesterday, arriving in Umm Qasr two days later. Iraq’s transport ministry has described the initiative as the national carrier’s first regular Gulf operation since the mid-1960s. The relaunch comes as Iraqi container supply chains have been radically reshaped since the Hormuz shipping crisis erupted at the end of February. Growing volumes have been diverted to Jordan’s Red Sea port of Aqaba before travelling overland into Iraq through the Trebil border crossing. candidates.title: NTSB releases preliminary report on Michigan switching fatality
candidates.excerpt: GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — An employee of a supplier of ready-mix concrete was killed on Sept. 21 when he was run over by multiple railcars during switching at the company’s facility in Grand Rapids, the National Transportation Safety Board said in its preliminary investigation report. The accident at High Grade Materials Co. occurred at 10:27 a.m. while a two-person crew was using a Trackmobile to move five loaded rail cars from a storage track to a loadout track. One crew member worked on the ground as a spotter while the second operated the Trackmobile. The driver told NTSB investigators that in their last radio communication, the spotter said he was setting a handbrake. The Trackmobile driver continued north with the cut of cars. The spotter was later found by the driver and his supervisor after the driver was unable to reach the other crew member. They were topped by metallic ores and metals typically used in steelmaking, 19.7%; forest products, 9.6%, and motor vehicles and parts, 9.4%.
